Q: SQL query performance: one query with a large WHERE clause, or many smaller separate ones? A:

For this scenario, using a Table‑Valued Parameter is the best practice.

It avoids long IN clauses, prevents multiple round‑trips to SQL Server,

and keeps the query fully set‑based and performant.

CREATE TYPE dbo.BarcodeList AS TABLE
(
    Barcode VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY
);

CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetBinStock
    @Barcodes dbo.BarcodeList READONLY
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT
        b.Barcode,
        b.Bin,
        b.Quantity
    FROM BinStock b
    JOIN @Barcodes bl
        ON b.Barcode = bl.Barcode;
END;

Q: Spark job fails with UnsafeExternalSorter OOM when using groupBy + collect_list + sort – how to optimize? A:

I dont have exact query of what you are trying to do...

AFAIK, This is not a Spark memory tuning issue... It is an unbounded per-key aggregation problem. Avoid collect_list on large groups. Use windowing with row_number to limit per-key data before grouping

for example :

WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT *,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY time_col) AS rn
  FROM table
)
SELECT key,
       collect_list(struct(time_col, value)) AS top_n
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 100
GROUP BY key

In the above query (most cases it should work ) Sorting happens distributed before grouping , Each group is capped ...No unbounded arrays

Q: Concurrent access to Java HashMap object A:

Cannot use HashMap

Java REST application where I'm using a HashMap to store some data

⚠️ Whoops, HashMap is the wrong class for that. HashMap is thread-safe only when the map is unchanging, read-only. But you said you are changing the map across threads. So you cannot safely use HashMap for your purpose.

ConcurrentMap

Given that you are accessing a changing map across threads, you must use a ConcurrentMap. If your keys are ordered, use a ConcurrentNavigableMap.

As for concrete implementations of those interfaces, these are bundled with Java:

  • If your keys are not ordered, use ConcurrentHashMap.
  • If your keys are ordered, use ConcurrentSkipListMap

Race conditions

Every request will make at least a Map.containsKey(someKey) and eventually a Map.get(someKey)

If a map is being modified across threads, then it makes no sense to call containsKey and later call get if you expect consistent results. In between those two calls the key that was found in the containsKey call may no longer be present in the map by the time of the get call.

This problem is known as a race condition.

Atomic operations

Instead of your approach, study the methods on ConcurrentMap to understand what methods operate atomically.

  • If you want to enter a value only if the specified key is not already associated with a value, call putIfAbsent.
  • If you want to replace an entry for a key only if currently mapped to some value, call replace.
  • If you want to always write to the map, call Map#put. Even if the given value is already mapped to the given key, the map is nevertheless affected.

equals & hashCode

Be very careful about defining a sensible override of Object#equals and consistent Object#hashCode on the classes of your key and value objects.

Q: Java Concurrent HashMap A:

ConcurrentSkipListMap

If you need a Sorted ConcurrentMap look at ConcurrentSkipListMap. Considering its complexity it is both non blocking and fast. To be more specific:

This class implements a concurrent variant of SkipLists providing expected average log(n) time cost for the
containsKey, get, put and remove operations and their variants.

ConcurrentSkipListMap implements SequencedMap, ConcurrentMap, ConcurrentNavigableMap, and more.

Q: Why does a filter that is only supposed to change the alpha channel affect the RGB channels as well? A:

According to the docs, SVG filters are applied on pre-multiplied RGBA values. This means that the color components have been multiplied by the alpha component. When feComponentTransfer is applied, the color channels are un-pre-multiplied in order to apply the filter.

Pre-multiplying the RGBA values creates rounding errors:

#00171F * 0.01 = #000000 (black)

#00171F * 0.02 = #000001 (dark blue)

#00171F * 0.03 = #000101 (dark greenish blue)

So after pre-multiplication, the colors are quite different, but they don't contribute a lot to the final image, so it doesn't matter.

feComponentTransfer, however, will undo the pre-multiplication before it's applied, and then redo it when it's done. Because you are inverting the alpha channel, you end up greatly amplifying the color differences:

#000001 / .02 = #000032

#000101 / .03 = #002121

When the pre-multiplying is undone, the resulting differences are very significant.
